item.description:
This update includes 3.3 and 3.3.1, which weren't released on their own: their changes are listed here too.
### Added - **Config Drift:** a new read-only module. **Read the Tenant** saves the tenant's ZIA configuration (and Client Connector's and Private Access's, when ticked) and compares it with the previous read, any saved read or a Policy Simulator snapshot: for each list, what was added, removed, renamed, moved (not every rule shifted by one insert) and turned on or off, and each changed field; settings field by field. A list that couldn't be read in either is named, never shown as all removed. Who changed what comes from the objects themselves and, on request, from ZIA's audit log (up to 30 days). Export as CSV. The newest 20 reads per tenant are kept on this Mac and also open in the Policy Simulator. Only reads: it never changes the tenant. - **Block Page & Logo:** brand ZIA's block and caution pages for the whole tenant: colours, font, width, a logo (PNG, JPEG, GIF and other common images, fitted and saved again under ZIA's 10 KB limit), headings and messages, a support email and phone, an acceptable use policy link, and whether the reason and company name show. Extra CSS for the page's classes, with anything that could load or run something refused. A preview that loads and runs nothing, then a dry run, Apply after review (one change, then activation) and Undo. It's not part of POV Start's Apply All. - **Cloud App Control per app:** on Rules, give Facebook, X, LinkedIn, ChatGPT, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Gemini, Claude, Google Drive, Dropbox or Box its own rule, with the actions picked from what the tenant offers for that app. Balanced keeps its LinkedIn rule; the other tiers add none unless you pick them. - **Microsoft 365 Copilot inspection:** Strict, Balanced and ZTH add an SSL Inspection rule that decrypts Microsoft 365 Copilot, on its own **Copilot-Domains** destination group, at rule 1 above Zscaler's predefined rules and the Office 365 One Click bypass, so DLP and AI controls see Copilot while the rest of Microsoft 365 stays uninspected. It uses the tier's certificate handling. AI Guard uses the same rule. - **Leftover rules removed:** the Dry Run page lists rules this Mac made in the tenant in an earlier run with this version or later, under the same prefix, that the plan no longer has (renamed in a newer version, or switched off on Rules), each with a **Keep** box. Rules from runs with earlier versions, such as LinkedIn's old Cloud App Control rule (now **CAC-App-LinkedIn**), are named there but not removed: delete them by hand if you no longer want them. Apply removes the ones not kept, last, and only when everything else was made: each is read again, must match what was made, and is saved whole on the run's record first; if one isn't removed as planned, the rest stay. Only rules this Mac's run records show it made are listed; a rule with the same prefix that someone else made is only named, and an allow rule a default deny needs, AI Guard's rules and rules made from a captured template are never removed. **Undo** creates them again at their old position, never twice, and undoing the earlier run then removes them. Apply stops if the leftovers changed since the dry run. - **Private Access, connector group location:** pick the App Connector Group's city when the wizard creates it (San Jose, CA, when you don't). With a city picked, a re-run moves the wizard's group there, and Undo moves it back. A group of the tenant's that you picked is never moved. - **Compliance frameworks, GLBA and NIST CSF 2.0:** two new frameworks on Internet Access's Framework step and on Customer Intake. **GLBA** (Finance) is the FTC Safeguards Rule for financial institutions the FTC oversees, such as mortgage lenders, finance companies, tax preparers and auto dealers that arrange financing (banks, credit unions, SEC-registered brokers and advisers, and insurers follow their own regulators' rules, which aren't mapped); its evidence cites safeguards for identified risks, access controls that protect customer information, and monitoring of user activity, and it adds DLP rules for customer financial data, Social Security numbers with names, card numbers and credentials. **NIST CSF 2.0** (Any industry) cites the Protect and Detect outcomes web security supports, such as protecting data in transit and monitoring networks, with the general DLP rules. Each rule cites only the outcomes it supports; the evidence shows what the policy configures, not that a control is met. The compliance pack and its alignment cover both, and AI Guard uses its General profile for them. - **Summary report as Word:** **Save as Word…** on Internet Access › Apply saves the summary report as a Word document to edit and send, with the same sections as the Markdown and printable versions. Nothing in the file links to or loads anything from the internet. - **Compliance pack in Word:** the control mapping report and the test plan by control can also be saved as Word documents, with the same content as their printable pages; the test plan has a Result column to fill in. - **Compliance pack alignment:** with a compliance framework, the pack shows **Aligned**, **Partial** or **Gaps**: how many of the framework's controls this app maps rules to are cited by a rule or settings group you have switched on, and which aren't. It follows your changes on the Rules page, and the control mapping report (printable and Word) starts with it. It describes what the policy configures, not an audit result. - **Prove it, why:** each result now follows the request's path: whether Client Connector's app profiles and the PAC files they use (and the ones ZIA hosts) send it around ZIA, whether SSL Inspection decrypts it, then the rule that decides. **Check Client Connector bypasses** (on by default) reads Client Connector's profiles, 4 of its about 100 calls an hour, and keeps them, with the PAC files, for 5 minutes; **Read again** reads them afresh. - **Prove it, expected result:** pick what the POV should do with the destination (blocked, allowed, caution, isolated, inspected or not inspected), on the card and on each runbook test. The result says whether the configuration agrees, doesn't, or can't tell (for example when a rule for some users could decide first, or the site is a cloud app whose Cloud App Control rules decide), in which case run the test. It's never a pass or fail: that stays yours. - **POV posture score:** a POV's page has a **Posture & coverage** tab. **Take start score** at the start of the POV and **Take end score** at the end: about 40 read-only checks of what a POV touches (SSL Inspection, threat protection, URL Filtering, Cloud Firewall, DNS, File Type Control, data protection, AI and cloud apps, advanced settings, Client Connector), each with what was found, what it means, what to do and the outcome, a 0–100 score with a maturity level, and what improved and what went back between the two. Checks the API client can't read are left out of the score, not counted against it. When the POV's rules are for a pilot group, the page and the report say which checks count only rules for everyone. The scores are saved with the POV and go into the summary report. - **What ZIA cannot see:** on the same tab, **Check coverage** lists every reason traffic isn't inspected that the configuration shows, biggest first: SSL Inspection's do-not-decrypt rules, Client Connector app profiles' DNS and IP exclusions and VPN gateways, profiles that tunnel only listed destinations, and the PAC files ZIA hosts that send traffic direct (read as text, never run). A list or PAC file that couldn't be read, or could be read only in part, is said so, never taken as no bypass. The last check is saved with the POV and goes into the summary report. The posture score, coverage and Prove it share one read of Client Connector's profiles for 5 minutes, and the card says when it was made; retaking a score can read them afresh. - **Customer rules that decide first:** Internet Access's dry run names the tenant's own rules above a POV rule that decide its traffic first: **Shadowed** (the POV rule never applies), **Decided in part** (some of its categories, apps or file types) or **Redundant** (it already does the same), each with why and what to do. A rule made in the ZIA portal for any protocol or method, which ZIA saves with each one listed, counts as any. Only what's certain is listed: rules for other users or groups, that match on something the check doesn't compare, or that are Cloud App Control rules naming other operations, such as uploads for a rule about viewing, are counted, and Zscaler-managed rules are named. A rule that redirects DNS to another gateway or isolates with another profile counts as a different result, and POV rules created switched off aren't checked. With admin ranking on, a rule of a higher rank counts as first wherever it sits. It never stops Apply: Apply checks again and shows what it found. POV Start's review shows it, the POV keeps the newest check, and the summary report lists every finding. - **Steps to finish by hand:** the dry run and Apply list what the API can't do: settings to set in the ZIA portal, rules left out entirely and why, turning on Smart Browser Isolation when a URL rule isolates, and, when an SSL rule inspects, checking that every test machine trusts the root certificate (Client Connector may have installed it without it being trusted). The summary report lists each once, and in a POV they become its follow-ups (a long one in parts, so nothing is cut off). - **DLP, more for healthcare:** HIPAA, HITRUST and the ZTH Ebook tier get three more rules: **PHI-Sensitive** (a specially protected condition, such as substance use, HIV, psychotherapy notes or a genetic result, with a patient identifier), **PHI-Narrative** (clinical note wording with a patient identifier) and **PHI-Bulk** (50 or more medical record numbers, Medicare Beneficiary Identifiers, Social Security numbers or dates of birth in one transfer). Like every DLP rule they start by monitoring. - **SaaS DLP and Email DLP:** two new modules on Customize, both off until you switch them on and both monitor only, on the same DLP engines as Endpoint DLP. **SaaS DLP** needs SaaS Security (CASB) and the customer's SaaS tenants onboarded in ZIA: it makes one rule per kind of app onboarded (files, mail, collaboration, CRM, IT service, code repositories, cloud storage, generative AI) that reports incidents for data at rest in those apps. **Email DLP** needs its subscription and outbound mail routed through Zscaler: one rule that logs sensitive data in that mail, which is still delivered. Neither follows a pilot group, and the dry run says so. A tenant without the subscription gets a warning or a skipped row, not a failure. Both cite each framework's monitoring controls, as Endpoint DLP does. Undo, Check for Drift and the Bulk Rule Manager cover them; the manager's **Load Rules** makes up to nine more reads for them. - **DLP test files:** the test kit and compliance pack have a file for the three new rules and for Source-Code (a short made-up Java class). The credentials file adds a made-up private key header and tokens; the CUI file adds legacy markings. - **Prove it, as a user or group:** pick a user or group from the directory (or type a user) and Prove it checks as them, on the card and every runbook test, so rules for a pilot group can decide instead of reading "can't tell". The result says who it checked as and with which groups, or that the user wasn't found. - **Bulk Test, who was simulated:** each row with a user says who was found, where and with which groups, or that the user wasn't found and the row ran with no groups, and the page warns when any user wasn't found. The results file has **User** and **User's groups** columns. - **About:** credits for ZeroTrustPanda's ZTP Policy Wizard and Policy Simulator, and for Jason Smith and Mike Preissner, whose ideas reached this app through ZTP Policy Wizard 2.8.
### Changed - **Block-QUIC at rule 1:** the Cloud Firewall rule that drops QUIC (so browsers fall back to inspected HTTPS) now goes at rule 1, above Zscaler's predefined rules, and a re-run moves it back there. Where ZIA doesn't allow rule 1, it goes right after the predefined rules with a warning. Undo puts its fields back but leaves it at the top. - **Allow-Web and Allow-NTP:** only Strict has them now, since its default deny needs them. - **Geo-blocking:** only outbound connections to high-risk countries are blocked; the rule dropping SSH, RDP and FTP coming from them is gone. - **ZTH:** newly revived domains are blocked and newly registered domains get a caution page; anonymizers are blocked by one rule instead of two. - **Allow-Collab:** leaves out Zoom, Webex, GoToMeeting and RingCentral when the plan turns on their UCaaS One Click setting, which then handles them. - **AI Guard:** when the tenant already drops QUIC with a rule for everyone, AI Guard uses it instead of making its own. The SSL step is the Copilot rule above, shared with Internet Access, and AI Guard's old **AIG-Inspect** rule is removed, saved on the run's record for Undo, only when this Mac's AI Guard records show it made it, the Copilot rule is in place and an Inspect All rule decrypts the other AI apps with no rule of yours above it that could skip them; otherwise it stays, with why. - **DLP, CUI-Markings:** also looks for the legacy markings FOUO, LES, SBU and distribution statements B to F, on one match (so its dictionary no longer counts "Controlled by:", which any document can say), and leaves out a document that also carries a decontrol marking such as "Approved for public release". Adding such a phrase takes a document out of the rule, even set to Block. - **DLP, Credentials:** also looks for private keys and cloud or SaaS access tokens in their published formats, on one match. Permissive stays on Zscaler's dictionary alone. - **DLP, Source-Code:** now looks for code structure with more than four statements, on two new dictionaries, instead of Zscaler's Source Code dictionary. It sees Java, C# and C, and C++ and JavaScript with an include of a named header or a `require`; it doesn't see Python, most Go, JavaScript that only uses `import` or C++ that only includes standard headers. Balanced now has it for most general and federal frameworks, at medium severity. It keeps monitoring under **Block all**; set the rule itself to Block to block it. - **DLP, runs over an earlier POV:** with update in place on, the wizard's Credentials, Source-Code and CUI engines from an earlier run are brought up to date, with the new dictionaries created first. Undo puts them back. A rule that combines dictionaries is left out, with the reason, when the tenant lacks a Zscaler dictionary it needs. - **Prove it, firewall checks:** SSH to China now knows its country, so a rule that goes by destination country is named as the one deciding. Results also name rules above with the same result whose conditions the check can't see, since the log may name one of them. - **DLP, rule order:** PHI-Bulk, PHI-Sensitive and PHI-Narrative come first, then rules that combine dictionaries, then rules on one dictionary, and Source-Code last. By Zscaler's documentation, web DLP stops at the first rule that matches unless Evaluate All Rules is on, so a broader rule above would take their matches, and Source-Code, which keeps monitoring under **Block all**, would let a code file holding data another rule blocks through. Over an earlier POV, new rules go below what's already there, so check the order in the ZIA portal. - **DLP rule descriptions:** shortened to fit ZIA's limit with the **[ZPW POV]** mark: a rule with a long list of dictionaries names the first few and how many more. - **Compliance evidence, ISO 27001 and SOC 2:** reviewed again against the latest reference profiles. ISO 27001 adds three controls: information security for cloud services (on the Cloud App Control rules), privacy of personal data (on the SSL inspection exemptions for health and finance sites) and secure authentication (on the Credentials DLP rule when it blocks); DNS tunnel, password-protected archive, Trusted Resolver, DoH and Advanced Threat Protection rules also cite the ISO controls they support. SOC 2 adds the Confidentiality criterion C1.1 on DLP rules set to Block (it counts only when the report covers Confidentiality), and DNS tunnel, archive, SSL inspection and Advanced Threat Protection rules cite more of the criteria they support. No rule changes, only what the evidence cites. - **Internet Access, descriptions:** every description the wizard sends (rules, the custom URL category, captured categories, network services, DLP dictionaries and engines) now ends with **[ZPW POV]**, so the wizard's objects can be told apart in the ZIA portal. A description over ZIA's 255 bytes is shortened, keeping the mark. Neither is a difference by itself: objects made before 3.3 aren't changed just to add it. - **Internet Access, Apply re-checks more:** Apply now also stops when a rule or object of the tenant's own in the lists the dry run read (rules, DLP engines and dictionaries, network services, custom URL categories) was added, removed or renamed since, or a rule was edited, moved or switched on or off, and names the lists. A rule or DLP engine that Apply updates is read again just before, and one changed since the dry run is left as it is and listed as failed while the rest goes on. - **Internet Access, ZIA's limits:** the dry run and Apply say how many changes Apply makes to ZIA, how long it takes and how many of this API client's about 400 changes an hour are left (counted by this app). Apply won't start when its plan doesn't fit, changes to Cloud App Control, Endpoint DLP and activation go about 10 a minute, and if ZIA asks Apply to wait long it stops there, without activating, with what it made on the run's record for Undo; the results and the summary report say the next activation makes those changes live. Undo and activation are never held back by the count. - **Internet Access, creates ZIA doesn't confirm:** when ZIA doesn't answer a create, the results say it may have been made and to check the tenant, for every kind of object. It's never looked up by name or sent again, what needs it isn't made, the next rule goes one position further down, and the run is still activated. - **Internet Access, checked after apply:** after activating, Apply reads the tenant once more and checks that every object it created or changed is there as planned, with the ID it recorded. The results, the summary report's follow-ups and POV Start name anything that doesn't match. - **Simulate as:** text typed with nothing picked is now used as a user when you click Simulate, and shows as the pick. Before, it was ignored and the destination was simulated with no user. - **Advanced Threat Protection:** Alert for Unknown/Suspicious C2 Traffic is now a step to finish by hand in the ZIA portal: ZIA accepted it through the API but left it off. - **AI Guard:** Apply asks in a dialog before it makes any change, as the other Apply pages do. - **POV Tests:** Isolated uncategorized sites and DNS tunnels blocked have no built-in Prove it destination, since the old ones proved something else: type one, such as a brand-new domain or the domain your tunnel tool uses. - **Apply page:** after an Apply, **Done** is the highlighted button; it clears the result so the next dry run can be applied.
### Security - **Policy Simulator snapshots:** Client Connector app profiles no longer keep their uninstall, disable, logout, exit or other passwords, passcodes, secrets, tokens and one-time passwords, in whatever form Client Connector includes them when the simulator loads them, so a saved snapshot never holds them; nor do the forwarding profiles and IP-based app definitions saved with them. Opening an older snapshot that has them drops them, and saving it again leaves them out. - **CSV files:** a cell that starts with spaces or quotes before a formula character is guarded too, for spreadsheets that trim spaces before reading a cell.
### Fixed - **Undo:** if a rule or object the run created or updated has to be left as it is (renamed since, say), Undo no longer activates, so a block rule can't go live without its allow rules. What it did stays pending: fix what it lists and Undo again, or activate in the portal. - **PAC files:** a script whose regular expression runs for a very long time no longer holds up a check or the app: after 5 seconds it counts as a file that couldn't be run. A very long answer is cut. - **PAC downloads:** a redirect to another server, or from HTTPS to HTTP, isn't followed, and a server asking for a sign-in gets none. - **Snapshots:** more spellings of a password, PIN or key are left out of what the app keeps and saves. - **Active POVs:** a damaged POV file's counts can't crash the page. - **SaaS DLP:** with a long rule prefix, each rule's name now fits ZIA's limit. - **Dry run:** warns when a combined DLP rule would use an earlier engine that stays as it is because updates are off. - **Customize:** the Policy modules rows no longer overlap. - **Prove it, DNS over HTTPS:** the Cloud App Control rule for DNS over HTTPS is picked as Cloud App Control picks it: the tenant's default rule comes last, admin ranking applies, and a rule limited to some users or locations above it is named as one that could decide first. Before, a default rule could be taken as the deciding one. - **Prove it, Office 365:** with Client Connector checked, its IP-based app definitions count for the Office 365 and other One Click rules, as in the Policy Simulator. - **Prove it, DNS:** a ZPA resolver rule ("ZPA Resolver for Locations") no longer makes every DNS result uncertain. It only redirects the domains of ZPA application segments, which Prove it doesn't read, so it's taken as not applying and named in a note; the Policy Simulator with ZPA loaded still checks it. - **Policy Simulator, Undo of a change:** when reading a list back returns no list, or one without the change's entries, Undo no longer writes it back, so it can't replace the tenant's list (an allowlist, for example) with an empty one. - **Active POVs:** a narrow window no longer cuts off the right side of a POV's page; the tab buttons become a menu when they don't fit. The POV plan no longer lists Private Access or Digital Experience when they're off. - **DLP test data:** the healthcare file's medical record numbers are now written as the MRN dictionary looks for them. - **Bulk Test:** a recommendation for a row no named rule decided says "the default rule" instead of an empty name. - **Policy Simulator, snapshots:** a snapshot file with a certificate expiry far beyond the year 9999, or a load time that isn't a date, no longer makes the app quit when it opens or is saved again.
